title: Hiding in plain sight? Russell Brand’s conviction poses tough questions for UK entertainment industry | CNN
text:
Source: CNN

Russell Brand, the disgraced British comedian and actor, was handed alengthy prison sentenceon Monday after being found guilty in a London court of raping a young fan and sexually assaulting three women.

In addition to his convictions and prison sentence, Brand’s name will be on the sex offenders’ register for life.

While that much is certain, other questions remain, including one that is worryingly familiar in the UK, a country that has seen the downfall of a host of celebrities accused of sexual offenses. How did he evade justice for so long?

The 51-year-old former stand-up comedian’s conviction and the flurry of reaction from those who once moved in his orbit comes at a time of heightened debate in Britain about the toxic mix of fame, power and abuse.

Britain’s Culture Secretary Lisa Nandy said Sunday that sexual abuse remained a problem in the media industry. “Hand on heart I can’t say ‌to you as the ⁠culture secretary that this is not happening today and in fact, if I had to wager, I would say it is,” she told the BBC.

She warned that women were often too afraid to report offenses as “speaking up has ​a very ‌heavy ​cost.”

Just this week, the popular TV show Married at First Sight UK wasaxedfollowing an investigation into rapeallegations, according to Channel 4, at the same time as British media reported that an unnamed celebrity is attempting toblockthe publication of his name in relation to sexual misconduct allegations.

After Brand’s guilty verdict, London’s Metropolitan Police superintendent said in a statement that as his profile grew during his acting and comedy career, “so too did his sense of entitlement.”

The Met police also confirmed investigations are continuing regarding two further allegations of rape made against Brand. Prosecutors are assessing whether to bring additional charges, according to Britain’s Press Association (PA).

“I hope this conviction sends a clear message that no one is above the law, no matter how famous or powerful they may be,” senior police officer Andy Furphy said.

But that statement has done little to hold back a wave of concern about the seeming immunity of some powerful figures to skirt accountability.

Responding to the verdict, British actress Sarah Solemani, who starred in the Bafta-winning sitcom “Him & Her,” said in an op-ed that Brand is finally facing justice but warned that other abusers are “still hiding in plain sight.”

She said the comedy industry has “for some strange reason, brought me into the close orbit of more than your average number of sexual predators, several of whom are still merrily working.”

“I had to pull a project from a company when I was informed it was common knowledge that a high-level exec was known for allegedly raping a colleague. Another famous comic had to pull a project when I informed them a legend they were working with was also an alleged rapist,” she wrote in theGuardianon Friday.

Comedian Katherine Ryan, who worked with Brand on a comedy show in 2018, also responded to the verdict, saying on her podcast that she felt “grief” and “relief,” while commending the bravery of the survivors who “came forward despite Russell Brand having fame, power, money (and) a legion of fans ready to attack them.”

As well as figures within the comedy circuit, British broadcasters have also found themselves in the crossfire.

After Brand’s conviction, the BBC issued a statement about the celebrity’s controversial stint at the broadcaster in the 2000s.

“We published a detailed report in January 2025 into how complaints about Russell Brand’s conduct were handled. This looked at eight allegations of misconduct while he worked here between 2006 and 2008. It was of great concern to us that some people felt unable to raise concerns about Brand’s behaviour,” a BBC spokesperson said.

“We apologised to those impacted, for both the culture and failings at the time, and we reiterate that apology again today,” the BBC said.

Brand’s convictions date back to 2004, 2005 and 2009, the decade when Brand moved from alternative comedy on a radically twisting path that took him to British television, Hollywood and eventually the world of podcasting and conspiracy theories.

In 2006, Brand began co-hosting “The Russell Brand Show” on BBC Radio 2, a weekly Saturday night program during which he had frank, comedic and often X-rated conversations with a co-host and guests.

However, the popular radio show ended abruptly two years later with Brand’s exit after the comedian and his co-host left a series of misogynistic voice messages for famed actor and “Fawlty Towers” star Andrew Sachs about his granddaughter.

During a live radio segment, Brand and his then-co-presenter Jonathan Ross made lewd remarks about Brand’s relationship with Sachs’ granddaughter, Georgina Baillie, with the incident prompting several resignations and sparking a national backlash.

Baillie sent her support to Brand’s victims following Thursday’s verdict while speaking about the devastating impact the BBC scandal had on her life.

“Justice has been served. Although he never raped or assaulted me as I have always said, I didn’t know what happened in the privacy of the rooms that the victims and Russell were in and their evidence was compelling,” she told Britain’s Daily Mailnewspaper. “I now want Russell to right the wrongs.”

Brand’s exposure represents the latest in a string of historic abuse investigations into former BBC stars, including sex offendersRolf HarrisandJimmy Savilewho were both staples of family television during their heyday.

“There can be no place for the abuse of power. Across the industry we must work together to ensure that anyone who suffers at someone else’s hand feels able to report it, that their concerns are taken seriously and that they are listened to,” the BBC’s statement said.

Allegations of rape and sexual assault against Brandwere made publicin a joint 2023 investigation by three British media outlets – The Sunday Times, The Times and Channel 4’s “Dispatches” program.

Brand has denied the allegations in the program, which related to multiple women who were not involved in the criminal trial.

Esella Hawkey, the executive producer of the documentary, “Russell Brand: In Plain Sight,” said she was pleased with the verdict but added that she “would much rather these events not have happened in the first place.”

Speaking about how Brand evaded justice for so long, Hawkey told CNN it can be “very difficult” for individuals to challenge “so-called talent and very big names who, you know, have a huge monetary value for the broadcasters.”

“I think television and broadcasting does have a problem with dealing with that behavior and also in enabling people,” she said. “I really do hope that this is an opportunity for the industry to do some inward looking.”

On Thursday, the director of news at Channel 4, Louisa Compton,said“the trial heard that women involved in the criminal case came forward after seeing the Channel 4 Dispatches film,” while commending the courage of the women involved.

The TV channel’s role in spotlighting the former comedian’s behaviour has not made it immune from criticism.

Following the 2023 revelations, Channel 4announcedit had opened an investigation into whether people at the channel were aware of Brand’s behavior while he was engaged in programs made for the broadcaster between 2004 and 2007.

The network said the investigation did not find any evidence to suggest Channel 4 employees were aware of Brand’s behavior documented in the expose, but then-CEO of Channel 4 Alex Mahon apologized over a separate allegation about Brand in 2009 that she said was not investigated as it should have been.

“In my view, it is a matter of regret for our industry that repugnant behaviours were tolerated – and indeed appeared on-air – in the past,” Mahonsaid.
